svg.title: Where on-demand stops being the cheaper option
svg.desc: On-demand DynamoDB capacity is billed per request at $0.625 per million writes and $0.125 per million eventually consistent reads. Provisioned capacity is billed per capacity unit per hour at $0.00065 per write capacity unit hour and $0.00013 per read capacity unit hour. Converting the provisioned rates to a per-million-request basis gives roughly eighteen cents per million writes and under four cents per million reads at full utilisation, so provisioned becomes cheaper above about twenty-nine per cent sustained write utilisation and about fourteen per cent for reads. Switching from provisioned to on-demand is limited to four times in a rolling twenty-four hour window, and switching in the console deletes auto scaling settings.
svg.text: TWO BILLING MODELS, PUT ON ONE SCALE
On-demand · billed per request
$0.625 per million writes
$0.125 per million reads (eventually consistent)
1 WRU per 1 KB written. Half an RRU per 4 KB read.
Transactions double both. Nothing to forecast.
Provisioned · billed per capacity unit-hour
$0.00065 per WCU-hour
$0.00013 per RCU-hour
1 WCU = one 1 KB write per second, held for an hour.
You pay for the reservation, used or not.
THE SAME RATES, CONVERTED TO ONE UNIT
A capacity unit held for an hour serves 3,600 requests. Divide the hourly rate by that.
WRITES provisioned $0.00065 / 3,600 = $0.18 per million on-demand $0.625 per million
On-demand costs about 3.5× more per write — so provisioned wins above roughly 29% sustained utilisation.
READS provisioned $0.00013 / 3,600 = $0.04 per million on-demand $0.125 per million
On-demand costs about 3.5× more per read too — identical to writes, so reads cross over at the same 29%.
WHICH MEANS THE ANSWER IS RARELY THE SAME FOR BOTH
Spiky, unpredictable, or new
On-demand. You cannot forecast what you have never
run, and idle provisioned capacity is pure waste.
Steady, known, and read-heavy
Provisioned with auto scaling. Read-heavy tables clear
the break-even long before write-heavy ones do.
The switch is not symmetric, and it is rate-limited
AWS allows a table to move from provisioned to on-demand only four times in a rolling 24-hour window. The reverse direction,
on-demand to provisioned, can be done at any time. Do not plan to chase load by flipping modes.
Switching in the console deletes your auto scaling settings
AWS documents that moving provisioned to on-demand in the console deletes all auto scaling settings, while the same change
made through the CLI or SDK preserves them. Identical operation, different outcome, decided by which tool you happened to use.
